A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same contamination-detection study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original contamination experiments, benchmark pass@1 scores, detector AUROCs, and training-objective ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds results for additional models, model sizes, detection methods, and task domains.

M1.justification: The two contamination procedures and the SFT, GRPO, RAFT, and RAFT++ objectives remain unchanged. Additional model configurations and the embedding-based comparator extend evaluation without revising the contamination method.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, v2 evaluates LiveCodeBench v2 for coding and six selected MMLU-Pro domains for general QA. Appendix E.11 reports both pre-LRM and post-LRM contamination experiments on this substantially broader task coverage.

E2.justification: The original ten detectors and training-objective controls are retained. v2 adds an evaluated embedding-based MLP detector following Liu et al. (2024), with AUROCs in Table 19; v1 only cited embedding methods and presented embedding visualizations.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 30K clean SFT samples and ninefold member duplication, Qwen 3B/14B configurations, and a 14B distilled reasoning model. v2 also adds a 280-step RL experiment and an embedding-classifier protocol using an 80/20 train/test split and hidden-layer selection. These extend the experimental design; the original shared settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analysis of response length as a possible confound (Figure 6), model-size sensitivity (Appendix E.6), and longer RL training testing whether task improvement coexists with concealment (E.7). It also supplements embedding visualizations with quantitative detection analysis (E.8). The original clipping and token-selection ablations remain.

E5.justification: The documented detection averaging over eight responses and pass@1 rollout counts are unchanged. Neither version reports training-seed replications, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new response-length boxplots describe variation across questions rather than uncertainty in experimental effects.

E6.justification: Original numerical table rows are retained, while substantial results are added for model families, sizes, longer training, embeddings, and non-math tasks. Newly reported examples include DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B pass@1 increasing from 59.83% to 69.24% after contamination (Table 4), and embedding-detector average AUROC decreasing from 66.31% to 50.66% after clean RL (Table 19). These are new experimental results, not cross-version performance gains.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1, the membership-gap definitions, algorithm-specific derivations, and the full proof in Appendix C are unchanged. The additional experiments introduce no new formal result.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are unchanged. Both versions claim that RL can conceal earlier SFT contamination, final-stage CoT contamination can evade existing detectors, and PPO-style importance sampling/clipping helps explain concealment.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies weak RL performance gains as a consequence of short training, argues that response length is not the main concealment driver, and distinguishes coding from general QA, where detection remains stronger (Appendices E.3, E.7, E.11). Quantitative embedding results also qualify v1's visual-only inference about indistinguishability. These substantially expand the interpretation and applicability boundaries, although Appendix A itself is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 documents the Llama-specific training-data recipe and adds UMAP parameters, embedding inputs, classifier splitting, and layer-selection details. The original SFT/RL hyperparameter tables, hardware disclosure, and code repository remain unchanged; the new reproducibility statement mainly points to existing material.

R1.justification: v2 adds Dominguez-Olmedo et al. (2024) to the contamination-concealment discussion and Dubey et al. (2024) for Llama 3. The main literature positioning and claim of investigating concealment at the algorithmic level remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section structure are retained. v2 makes localized rewrites, reorders related-work paragraphs and appendix material, adds an appendix contents page and stage labels, and introduces acknowledgements, reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: Tables 1, 4, and 5 expand to include additional models. v2 adds a Llama detection-trend chart, response-length boxplots, and substantial new tables for model-size, training-duration, embedding, and domain experiments. Existing figures are retained and relocated, with some revised captions; these are distinguishable from the genuinely new displays.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis by addressing v1's reliance on one pre-LRM base model, math/science evaluation, and visual-only embedding evidence. Model-family and size checks, non-math evaluations, response-length analysis, longer-training controls, and quantitative embedding detection address important generality and validity gaps. Some broad near-random-detection wording remains insufficiently qualified by the stronger general-QA results in Table 22, but the added evidence and applicability distinctions provide a substantial net improvement.
